course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments that occurred before 1519 provides the most relevant historical context for the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire?
choices: The founding of Jamestown in 1607, which showed European monarchies that overseas colonies could be profitable and permanent
The Aztec decision to build Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, which later gave Spain a defensible base
The completion of the Reconquista in 1492, which linked Spanish military expansion to the spread of Christianity
The Spanish decision to end exploration after the failure of Columbus's voyages to reach Asia directly
questions.explanation: The Reconquista ended in January 1492 and tied the Spanish monarchy's military power to Christian expansion, which helps explain the conquest.
choiceExplanations: Jamestown was a real development, but it came almost ninety years after the conquest, so it cannot be context from before.
The Aztec island capital did not give Spain a base; Spanish forces had to fight their way into it.
The Reconquista ended in January 1492 and tied the Spanish monarchy's military power to Christian expansion, which helps explain the conquest.
Spain did not end exploration after Columbus; it expanded its voyages and conquests.
questions.distinguisher: Both Jamestown and the Reconquista involve European expansion, but only the Reconquista came before 1519 and so can be context from before the conquest.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Native American societies in North America before 1491 are best described as
choices: diverse societies that adapted to their environments through varied farming, resource use, and social structures
mostly mobile hunter-gatherer groups that moved with the seasons and rarely built permanent settlements or large towns
politically united societies governed by a single alliance that controlled the Atlantic coast and the interior
isolated communities that avoided trade and contact with distant peoples because of geographic barriers
questions.explanation: Native peoples developed distinct and increasingly complex societies by adapting to and transforming their varied environments.
choiceExplanations: Native peoples developed distinct and increasingly complex societies by adapting to and transforming their varied environments.
Many societies farmed or lived in permanent villages, and some built large towns, so ways of life differed widely by region.
No single alliance governed North America; societies had many separate political systems.
Many societies, such as Mississippian peoples, took part in long-distance trade networks.
questions.distinguisher: Some societies were mobile hunter-gatherers, but describing all of them that way ignores farming societies and permanent villages.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Portugal sent ships along the Atlantic coast of Africa in the 1400s?
choices: Portuguese rulers wanted land for settlers who had been displaced by religious conflict after the Protestant Reformation
African kingdoms asked Portugal to help defend their trade routes against rival Native American empires
Portugal hoped to replace the Mediterranean grain trade with crops that could be grown in West Africa
The Portuguese monarchy sought direct access to African gold and a sea route that avoided middlemen in Asian trade
questions.explanation: Portugal's rulers backed voyages to reach African gold and to find a sea route to Asian markets without paying intermediaries.
choiceExplanations: The Reformation began in 1517, after Portugal's voyages along Africa had started.
African states did not have contact with Native American empires in this period.
Portugal's goals centered on gold, trade goods, and sea routes, not replacing the grain trade.
Portugal's rulers backed voyages to reach African gold and to find a sea route to Asian markets without paying intermediaries.
questions.distinguisher: The Reformation was a major source of religious conflict, but it began in 1517, after Portugal's voyages were already under way.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following earlier developments best helps explain the later use of enslaved Africans on American plantations?
choices: The Muslim conquest of Iberia in the 700s, which introduced the practice of slavery to Europe for the first time
Sugar plantations on Atlantic islands such as Madeira and São Tomé that relied on enslaved African labor
The Protestant Reformation, which led several European churches to approve of slavery in the colonies
The Inca practice of the mita, which supplied rotating labor to farms across the Atlantic islands
questions.explanation: Portuguese and Spanish colonists tested plantation agriculture based on enslaved labor on Atlantic islands before it spread to the Americas.
choiceExplanations: Slavery already existed in Europe, Africa, and the Mediterranean, so the conquest did not introduce it.
Portuguese and Spanish colonists tested plantation agriculture based on enslaved labor on Atlantic islands before it spread to the Americas.
The Reformation did not create the plantation labor model, and it began after the island plantations existed.
The mita was an Andean labor system and was not used on Atlantic island farms.
questions.distinguisher: Slavery long predated the Atlantic voyages, but the island sugar plantations are the direct model for plantation labor in the Americas.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: A student is asked why Spain colonized parts of the Americas. Which of the following would serve best as a historical context for the response?
choices: The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire in 1532, which brought huge quantities of Andean silver to Spain
The decline of Native populations after smallpox epidemics, which weakened resistance to Spanish rule
Competition among European monarchies for wealth, trade routes, and religious influence in the late 1400s
The growth of enslaved labor on North American tobacco farms, which supplied crops to European markets
questions.explanation: Rivalry among European monarchies for wealth, trade, and religious influence was the wider setting in which Spain chose to colonize.
choiceExplanations: This is a result of colonization and a part of the topic, not a setting that came before it.
Epidemics were an effect of contact and helped the conquest; they are not the broader setting before colonization.
Rivalry among European monarchies for wealth, trade, and religious influence was the wider setting in which Spain chose to colonize.
Tobacco plantations in English colonies came later and are not context for Spain's early colonization.
questions.distinguisher: The conquest of the Inca is connected to Spanish colonization, but it is an example of the topic itself rather than a context that explains it.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Cahokia, a large settlement near present-day St. Louis, is best used as evidence that
choices: Native societies built cities only after they came into contact with Spanish colonists and missionaries
some Native societies built large urban centers supported by agriculture and trade before European contact
Native societies in the Mississippi Valley relied exclusively on hunting and gathering for their food
all Native societies in the Americas lived in large permanent cities connected by roads and trade
questions.explanation: Cahokia's mounds, farming, and trade network show that complex urban societies existed in North America before Europeans arrived.
choiceExplanations: Cahokia flourished centuries before sustained European contact.
Cahokia's mounds, farming, and trade network show that complex urban societies existed in North America before Europeans arrived.
Mississippian peoples farmed, and farming helped support Cahokia's size.
Many societies were smaller or mobile, so Cahokia is evidence of one form of complexity, not of all.
questions.distinguisher: Cahokia shows that large cities existed, but it does not show that every Native society lived in one.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments of the late 1400s best illustrates the competition among European states that preceded Columbus's first voyage?
choices: Portugal's progress down the African coast, which encouraged Spain to look for its own route to Asian trade
England's colony at Roanoke, which pressured Spain to claim the Caribbean islands before others could
The Dutch West India Company's charter, which ended Portuguese control of Atlantic shipping routes
The Aztec Triple Alliance's demand for tribute, which pushed Spain to look for new allies in Asia
questions.explanation: Portuguese voyages down Africa's coast raised the stakes for Spain, whose rulers then supported Columbus's western voyage in 1492.
choiceExplanations: Portuguese voyages down Africa's coast raised the stakes for Spain, whose rulers then supported Columbus's western voyage in 1492.
Roanoke was founded in 1585, long after Columbus's first voyage.
The Dutch company was created in 1621, well after this competition began.
The Aztec alliance had no contact with Spain before 1519 and did not drive Spanish exploration.
questions.distinguisher: Each choice names a later European or Native development, but only Portugal's voyages were happening before 1492.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how the Reconquista of 1492 is situated within the broader context of Spanish exploration?
choices: It removed Portugal as a rival and gave Spain sole control of Atlantic trade and exploration for the next century
It converted Muslim rulers to Christianity and ended religious conflict throughout western Europe
It created the first Spanish colonies in the Americas and shaped their labor systems and trade
It ended centuries of Christian-Muslim conflict in Iberia and freed the monarchy to pursue expansion overseas
questions.explanation: The fall of Granada ended the long struggle with Muslim states in Iberia and let the monarchy turn its resources and religious zeal toward expansion.
choiceExplanations: Portugal remained a strong rival, which is why the two states later negotiated the Treaty of Tordesillas.
The Reconquista did not end religious conflict; the Protestant Reformation soon created new conflict.
The Reconquista took place in Iberia, not in the Americas.
The fall of Granada ended the long struggle with Muslim states in Iberia and let the monarchy turn its resources and religious zeal toward expansion.
questions.distinguisher: Portugal was indeed a rival, but the Reconquista did not remove it; Spain and Portugal divided the Atlantic world by treaty in 1494.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.
